title: Holding the Line
passage:
A queue has no warden, no charter and no penalty clause, and yet it remains among the most reliably obeyed ___(1)___ in public life. The whole arrangement runs on little more than a shared ___(2)___ that everybody present will keep the place they took. When the behavioural researcher Ingrid Mautner spent three winters watching ticket halls, bakeries and ferry gangways in four European cities, what struck her was not that people queued but how little instruction they needed in order to do it. Newcomers read the shape of a line — its angle to the counter, the width of the gaps between shoulders, the direction the bodies face — and slot themselves into it without a word being exchanged. Where that shape is ambiguous, the trouble starts: a counter approached from two sides, she found, produced more open disputes in an afternoon than a roped corridor produced in a month.

___(3)___, the room itself does a good deal of the moral work that we prefer to credit to the people standing in it. The sanctions a queue can bring to bear are absurdly small — a tightening of the shoulders, a cough, a stare held half a second too long. They are usually enough. Mautner is careful about how far she pushes the finding. Her cities were few and her winters were cold, and cold weather, she remarks drily, shortens everybody's temper.

What keeps a line intact, on her evidence, is not ___(4)___ at all. The people in it are cold, impatient and privately sure that the counter could be staffed better; they hold their places anyway, because the alternative is to be looked at. Where a queue does break down, it is seldom because somebody has decided to be rude. It is because the shape stopped being ___(5)___ — a second till opened, a rope was moved, a doorway offered two equally honest ways in — and thirty people discovered at the same moment that they no longer agreed about where the line was.
— Perpetua Rooke, society notebook

questions.rationale: Collocation gap; all four are plural abstract nouns in con-…-ions (POS-uniform, shape-matched). The frame 'it remains among the most reliably obeyed ___ in public life', set against 'no warden, no charter and no penalty clause', needs a noun naming an unlegislated rule that people nonetheless follow: 'obeyed conventions' is the locking collocation and it is what the whole passage goes on to describe. convictions = collocation_misfit (a conviction is one's own belief; one holds or acts on convictions, one does not obey them, and they are not shared public rules). concessions = collocation_misfit (a concession is something granted or given up; 'obeyed concessions' is not English). connections = sense misfit (links between things or people, not rules that can be obeyed). Only 'conventions' is idiomatic in the frame; the other three are real nouns of the same shape that fail on sense or collocation.

Collocation gap with a suffix-rhymed -umption set. The frame 'runs on little more than a shared ___ that everybody present will keep the place they took' needs a noun that takes a that-clause naming something taken for granted: 'a shared assumption that…' locks. resumption = collocation_misfit (a resumption is the restarting of something and takes 'of', not a that-clause: 'a shared resumption that…' is not English). consumption = sense misfit (using up goods; it cannot govern a that-clause about how people will behave). gumption = sense/collocation misfit (initiative or nerve, an uncountable quality that is not 'shared … that…'). Only 'assumption' fits both the syntax of the frame and the argument, since the passage insists nothing here is enforced.

Connective-logic gap; all four are sentence-initial adverbs of the same connective class. The sentence immediately before supplies the evidence — an ambiguous counter 'produced more open disputes in an afternoon than a roped corridor produced in a month' — and the gapped sentence draws the conclusion the writer wants from it ('the room itself does a good deal of the moral work…'). The link is therefore consequential: 'Accordingly'. Admittedly = wrong_logic (concessive; it would mark the claim as a point against the writer's own line, whereas the design claim is the writer's conclusion). Conversely = wrong_logic (demands an opposite, but the sentence extends the previous one rather than reversing it). Nevertheless = wrong_logic (signals a contrast with what precedes; nothing here is being overridden). Only 'Accordingly' matches the inference the evidence sentence sets up.

Polarity gap. The frame 'What keeps a line intact, on her evidence, is not ___ at all' negates the gap, so the word in it must be the warm, positive-pole quality the reader would otherwise credit — and the next sentence supplies the proof by naming its opposite: the people 'are cold, impatient and privately sure that the counter could be staffed better; they hold their places anyway'. 'Courtesy' is the quality being denied. hostility = polarity_mirror (a skimmer grabs the negative-pole word because 'cold' and 'impatient' sit beside the gap, but 'not hostility at all' would claim the queuers are not unfriendly, which the very next clause contradicts). curiosity = sense misfit and a second polarity trap (it is neither the warm virtue being denied nor anything the evidence bears on). vanity = sense misfit (self-regard is not what anyone would suppose holds a queue together, so denying it explains nothing). Only 'courtesy' makes the negation do the work the following sentence supports.

Collocation gap with a suffix-rhymed -(l)igible set, keyed to the passage's own metaphor: newcomers 'read the shape of a line'. The frame 'It is because the shape stopped being ___', glossed by the breakdowns that follow (a second till, a moved rope, 'a doorway offered two equally honest ways in'), needs the adjective for something that can no longer be read: 'legible'. illegible = polarity_mirror ('stopped being illegible' would mean the shape had become readable, the opposite of what the collapse requires). eligible = sense misfit (qualified to be chosen; a shape is not eligible for anything). negligible = sense misfit (so small as not to matter, which says nothing about whether the queue can be read). Only 'legible' completes the reading metaphor the first paragraph plants.
